storyboard.claim: The scariest part is not the vampire — it is your husband dismissing you for noticing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia trying to warn Carter, who turns away from her with crossed arms.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cold open.
storyboard.addedInformation: Two characters on screen establish the marital dynamic before any monster is mentioned.

storyboard.claim: The real horror of this novel is what we are examining today.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia walking alone down a manicured suburban street — the world that will devour her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the husband's dismissal to the broader thesis: this is a horror story about something deeper.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pristine street and her solitary figure set the suburban-horror tone.

storyboard.claim: A literal monster moves into a pristine neighborhood.
storyboard.concreteVisual: James Harris arriving on the manicured street — the home icon grounds Mount Pleasant as a domestic space he enters.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the general horror thesis to the specific event: the monster moves in.
storyboard.addedInformation: James's polished smile beside the home icon says the neighborhood is the setting he will infiltrate.

storyboard.claim: The neighborhood's social contract depends on women's labor being invisible.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia standing in her kitchen holding a casserole — the visible symbol of the invisible labor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the monster arriving to the system he will exploit: the women's unseen work.
storyboard.addedInformation: The casserole in her hands is the object the suburb runs on but never acknowledges.

storyboard.claim: James Harris does not break the rules — he exploits infrastructure already built for exploitation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: James as the puppeteer — he controls the strings that were already attached to the women.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the invisible labor to who benefits: James simply pulls existing strings.
storyboard.addedInformation: The puppeteer icon says he controls people through a system, not through force.

storyboard.claim: This is not a standard Gothic Dracula story with a monster in a misty castle.
storyboard.concreteVisual: No castle, no mist — the struck-through text rejects the Gothic framing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After naming what the story IS, now crossing out what it is NOT.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike tells a muted viewer this genre expectation is being dismissed.

storyboard.claim: We are planted in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, late 1980s into the 1990s — manicured lawns and blooming azalea bushes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia on a pristine suburban street — the home icon grounds us in domestic Mount Pleasant.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From rejecting the Gothic framing to establishing the real setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the place and era a muted viewer needs to orient.

storyboard.claim: This society is devastatingly, aggressively polite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two suburban women smiling at each other with the mask icon — politeness as a facade, not genuine warmth.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the physical setting to its social texture: forced smiles everywhere.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask beside two smiling women says the politeness is performed, not felt.

storyboard.claim: Our protagonist Patricia Campbell lives with her husband Carter, an ambitious psychiatrist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia and Carter together in their home — introducing the couple.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the world to the protagonist who lives in it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the main character for a muted viewer.

storyboard.claim: Patricia's life is a never-ending loop of carpools, casserole deliveries, and managing her mother-in-law.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia in the kitchen holding a casserole dish — the loop of domestic labor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From naming Patricia to showing what her life actually consists of.
storyboard.addedInformation: The casserole in her hands makes the domestic labor cycle concrete.

storyboard.claim: To escape suffocating perfection, Patricia joins a local women's book club.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia and Slick sitting in the living room with a book — the club is her escape.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the grinding routine to what breaks it: the book club.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book icon beside seated women names what they do together.

storyboard.claim: They pretended to read heavy literary classics — but quickly abandoned that facade.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Book club women holding a respectable book, but they replaced the literary classics with true crime.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From joining the club to what they pretended to read — and didn't.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike tells a muted viewer the literary classics were dropped.

storyboard.claim: They gleefully switched to trashy true-crime paperbacks — and a charming parasitic stranger arrives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The women happily holding books with the true-crime paperback icon — the blood-splattered cover shows what they actually read.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From rejecting the boring books to what replaced them.
storyboard.addedInformation: The custom true-crime icon with its blood splatter matches the subversive reading the narrator names.

storyboard.claim: James Harris arrives — and to understand why he is so successful, you must see Patricia's life before the supernatural enters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: James walking confidently into the neighborhood — his polished smile is the first thing the viewer sees.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the bored housewives to the predator who enters their world.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the antagonist and shows his charming exterior.

storyboard.claim: Imagine Patricia sitting on Marjorie Fretwell's enormous, suffocating pink sofa.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia sitting awkwardly on a sofa in the chintz living room — sweating, dread-filled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From James's arrival to rewinding to Patricia's life before him.
storyboard.addedInformation: The specific object (pink sofa) grounds this in the narrator's own scene.

storyboard.claim: Patricia is supposed to lead a scholarly discussion, but she has not read a single page.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia sitting frozen, holding a book she hasn't opened — the dread of being exposed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the pink sofa scene: what Patricia is feeling on it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book in her hands and her worried face say she is unprepared and terrified.

storyboard.claim: She has not read a single page because her life is a relentless cascade of invisible domestic crises.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia slumping in the kitchen — the chains icon shows invisible domestic labor binding her in an endless loop of tasks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From her dread to why: the cascade of crises that consumed her reading time.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chains icon turns 'relentless domestic labor' into a visible constraint chaining her to the kitchen.

storyboard.claim: Her son Blue shoved 24 raisins up his nose, requiring frantic medical attention.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia reaching toward a child in panic — the medical icon says this required a doctor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First specific crisis in the cascade: a medical emergency.
storyboard.addedInformation: The absurd concrete detail (24 raisins) instantly communicates the chaos.

storyboard.claim: Her mother-in-law moved in, requiring constant, grueling, unglamorous care.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia tending to an elderly figure — the family icon says this is a family obligation, not a choice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second crisis in the cascade: the mother-in-law.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's own phrase names the labor that no one thanks her for.

storyboard.claim: Patricia literally beat a snake to death with a rake in the garage room toilet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia recoiling from a coiled snake — the custom snake icon shows the literal animal she killed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Third and most extreme crisis in the cascade: a snake in her own home.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book's own signature object — the first literal monster, foreshadowing the real one.

storyboard.claim: She sits on that sofa feeling like a hollowed-out shell, drained of her own identity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia slumped on the sofa, completely depleted — no icon needed, the body tells it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the cascade of crises: the result on Patricia herself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her posture (slumped, sad) shows the emotional cost of everything before.

storyboard.claim: Hendrix establishes that the exhausting, unacknowledged domestic grind IS the baseline horror.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia alone on an abstract backdrop — the thematic beat isolates her from the domestic setting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the specific crises to the narrator's thesis about what they mean.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phrase names the argument: domestic life is already horror before any vampire.

storyboard.claim: Before a literal vampire drains her blood, her environment and family have already drained her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-step flow: environment -> family -> vampire, all draining Patricia.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The baseline horror becomes a causal chain: she is drained at every level.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flow shows three layers of the same verb (drain) the narrator stacks.

storyboard.claim: She is already a victim — her life force consumed daily to keep the suburb running.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia slumped, drained — no icon, her body tells the story of depletion.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Conclusion of the drain chain: she was a victim before James arrived.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phrase pins the thesis: victimhood preceded the supernatural.

storyboard.claim: Beating a snake to death in a toilet is just considered another Tuesday.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia holding a casserole in the kitchen with the snake icon — she killed a snake and is still expected to cook.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From 'already a victim' to the darkly comic proof: the snake was routine.
storyboard.addedInformation: The casserole beside the snake says she went straight from killing an animal to domestic duty.

storyboard.claim: The domestic space is already a site of intense, unacknowledged violence and exhaustion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia in the kitchen with a casserole — the domestic space where violence is absorbed and ignored.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the snake being routine to the thesis: domestic space is violent, but no one names it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's phrase makes the hidden violence explicit for a muted viewer.

storyboard.claim: It is not isolated to Patricia — look at Slick Paley, another book club member.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Slick Paley alone in a room — introducing a second woman crushed by the same system.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Patricia's domestic violence to another woman suffering the same thing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the new character for a muted viewer.

storyboard.claim: Slick is so overwhelmed by maternal expectations that she methodically batch-prepares.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Slick in a kitchen holding a casserole dish — overwhelmed by the volume of what motherhood demands.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From introducing Slick to what is crushing her: the sheer volume of mothering.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her worried face and the casserole say she is drowning in domestic labor.

storyboard.claim: She makes and freezes 60 sandwiches on the first Monday of every month.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Slick in the kitchen with the food icon — she is literally mass-producing meals.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the general maternal overwhelm to the specific, absurd number.
storyboard.addedInformation: The number 60 and the food icon make the scale of this labor absurdly concrete.

storyboard.claim: She freezes them so she can blindly throw one into her kids' lunch boxes every morning.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Slick reaching into a freezer — the mechanical, mindless repetition of morning lunch prep.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the batch production to its purpose: a daily mechanical grab.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reaching action and the narrator's phrase show automation as survival.

storyboard.claim: It is like someone on a sinking ship furiously bailing water with a thimble.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Slick alone on an abstract backdrop — the narrator's metaphor is too vivid to need an icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the mechanical action to the narrator's metaphor for how futile it is.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phrase captures the hopelessness the narrator intends — no icon reads as 'futile coping'.

storyboard.claim: She is desperately building a hyper-efficient assembly line to survive — a survival tactic masquerading as domestic efficiency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Slick in the kitchen holding a casserole, looking frantic — efficiency as desperation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the thimble metaphor to its meaning: this is survival, not homemaking.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes the sandwiches as combat strategy, not choice.

storyboard.claim: Challenge: isn't this just normal chaotic 1990s parenting?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A generic figure speaking — posing the counterargument that this is all ordinary.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Slick's survival mode to a pushback: maybe this is just how things are.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question mark in the callout signals doubt, not a conclusion.

storyboard.claim: It is like a CPU running at 99% — bogged down but doing what it was designed to do.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia on an abstract backdrop, the CPU metaphor expressed through the callout text.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the counterargument with an analogy: overloaded but functional.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the CPU metaphor is the narrator's, but no icon renders it — the text carries it alone.

storyboard.claim: It is frustrating, but it is just the operating system doing what it is designed to do.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia standing neutral — the system is working as intended, even if she is exhausted.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the CPU analogy: the system is not broken, it is designed this way.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the continuation extends the computer metaphor without new visual information.

storyboard.claim: You could argue this is not horror — it is just the mundane reality of raising a family. Stressful but not uniquely malicious.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The counterargument speaker — it is stressful but maybe not evil.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The counterargument peaks: maybe there is no horror here, just stress.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question mark preserves the challenge; this is not the narrator's conclusion.

storyboard.claim: The distinction between normal stress and malicious erasure is exactly where the true horror lies — it crosses the line because of how the men perceive and categorize this labor.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum from normal stress to malicious erasure, weighted far toward erasure — the answer to the challenge.
storyboard.onScreenText: NORMAL STRESS ← → MALICIOUS ERASURE (spectrum, value near erasure)
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly answers the counterargument: it is not stress, it is erasure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The spectrum shows the distinction the narrator draws — the value near erasure says this is not normal.

storyboard.claim: Carter actively refers to Patricia's life as 'doing nothing.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Carter smiling and talking dismissively while Patricia stands behind him — he is mocking her work.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the abstract spectrum to the concrete proof: Carter's own words.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike-through says the narrator rejects Carter's framing — she is not doing nothing.

storyboard.claim: Carter jokes that her life is a mystery novel titled 'Patricia Campbell and The Secret of Cooking Three Meals a Day.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Carter talking with a smirk in the kitchen while Patricia stands exhausted behind him — his condescending joke about her invisible labor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From 'doing nothing' to the specific joke that proves his contempt.
storyboard.addedInformation: Carter's happy expression beside Patricia's exhaustion shows who finds this funny and who pays for it.

storyboard.claim: He leverages her invisible labor to build his career while mocking the effort — it is a social contract demanding her absolute invisibility.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia and Carter on an abstract backdrop — the chains icon says she is bound by a contract she cannot escape.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Carter's joke to the system it reveals: she must be invisible for his success.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chains say the invisibility is not a choice but a binding — domestic servitude disguised as marriage.
